title: Sonnet 18
author: William Shakespeare
text:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date;
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd;
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd;
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st;
Nor shall death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
who: William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) was an English playwright and poet, born in Stratford-upon-Avon and working mostly in London. This sonnet belongs to a sequence of 154 published together in 1609.
why: Who the poem addresses, and what prompted it, is not known. The sequence is traditionally read as speaking first to a young man and later to a dark-haired woman, but the identities are not documented, so any specific backstory would be guesswork.
notice: Count the first eight lines: the poem keeps listing the ways summer falls short. Then look at line nine, where it turns and starts promising something summer cannot, a kind of permanence. Ask what the poem says will do the preserving, and who gets the credit.
prompts: What is one ordinary thing from today you would want to keep from fading, and what would it take to keep it?
The speaker promises permanence through writing. What have you written, or wish you had written down, that has outlasted the day?
